title: Manic
full_review:
The troubled lives of adolescents at a juvenile mental institution are graphically explored in "Manic" (IFC). While dealing with important questions about violence and alienation among today's youth, the in-your-face rawness of this disturbing film by Jordan Melamed may prove to be more than a bit off-putting.

Lyle (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is a volatile teen prone to fits of rage, the most recent resulting in his almost beating a classmate to death with a baseball bat. Committed to an institution in lieu of criminal prosecution, Lyle encounters Dave (Don Cheadle), a caring psychiatrist and reformed drug addict, who serves as ringmaster for the hospital's often emotionally charged group therapy sessions.

Eschewing a traditional narrative, the film mostly revolves around these rap sessions where the kids struggle to exorcise their personal demons through candid -- and quite often ear-splittingly vulgar -- exchanges. The discussions serve to heal as well as harm, with participants lashing out with lewd tirades, venting their misplaced anger at the only available targets. Included in the group is Chad (Michael Bacall), a bipolar, self-mutilating teen who befriends Lyle; Kenny (Cody Lightning), Lyle's sexually abused and painfully shy roommate; and Mike (Elden Henson), the bully of the bunch.

Lyle, tentative at first, slowly begins to respond to Dave's overtures. Yet each step forward leads inevitably into a revolving door of violent outbursts. Beleaguered by his own frustrations, Dave counsels Lyle that there are no panaceas, no easy epiphanies that will cure him, reminding him that learning to cope with his darker impulses is a lifelong battle. As Lyle tries to come to terms with his inner tempest, he begins to confide in Tracey (Zooey Deschanel), a withdrawn suicidal girl whose fragile psyche welcomes his affection.

However, when Chad stabs a guard, Lyle's tenuous placidity quickly and violently shatters. He erupts, taking his fury out on Mike, who had been egging him on. Lyle escapes but returns soon after, realizing he can never outrun himself.

Thematically, the filmmaker was inspired by Albert Camus'
"The Myth of Sisyphus," an existential essay based on the Greek mythological figure condemned forever to roll a boulder up an incline, only to watch it slide back down. The piece -- which Chad is seen reading in one scene -- questions whether life is an endless circle of absurdity, or whether people can journey toward meaning. Camus, a professed atheist, ultimately concluded that the world is devoid of any meaning, except that which people create for themselves through their personal choices. This fallacious and inherently pessimistic view is categorically inconsistent with Christian teachings concerning a divinely ordained purpose for existence.

It must be stated clearly that this film is not easy viewing. The sexually explicit language is odious and the violence which unfolds, shot in digital format to enhance its cinema-verite style, is graphic. However, much of what happens on screen is a physical acting-out of the teens' inner turmoil. To dismiss this film because of its offensive elements, while understandable, might miss an opportunity to see the diamond inside the coal -- a mistake by society that sometimes leads real-life teens down the self-destructive paths depicted.

Dave embodies a true Christian response to the woundedness encountered in "Manic." In spite of his misgivings he remains a healing, life-affirming presence. Where there is darkness he brings light, if only a flickering flame -- knowing well that it can be tragically extinguished at any moment. Though wrestling daily with despair and the seeming futility of his vocation, he refuses to give up, seeing beneath the teens' repellent facade a sacred humanity worthy of love.

As he observes during one of the group sessions, "love gives life meaning."

Due to recurring graphic violence and incessant rough and sexually explicit language as well as vulgarities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
